tile-domain.look: Reads immediately as the real thing on every pattern. Stretcher brick, herringbone and basket parquet with grain following each plank, hex tiles, chevron wood, random-course stone walls where every stone has its own length and height while courses stay level, fish scales, and fan cobbles that look like real European paving once each ring and fan gets a random phase. Hillshade shows crisp bevels. TiltedHeight gives sunken and tilted flagstones in the relief view. Noise on Mortar eats the brick edges into worn masonry. An upstream warp gives hand-laid stone. Nesting works: herringbone inside hexes, herringbone inside basket blocks. The stand-in wood Source is the weakest part of the parquet images: it is stylised stripes, not real wood, and that is the Source's fault, not the node's. Nothing on the existing contact sheet does any of this.
tile-domain.dims: 2D measured for all 9 patterns. 3D measured: zlen>0 cuts real boxes along z with staggered bond (a brick block with mortar on all faces; no jump along z), zlen=0 extrudes (hex prisms). 4D not run: the pattern lives in (x,y) and extra axes pass to the Source. Integer Period closes for tiling (worst 0.001, Fan 0.010, at P=24).

tile-domain.artifacts: Axis aligned by design, so the FFT shows a cross (axis 84 on the herringbone sheet). Without Bevel, value outputs jump 1 to 2 at tile edges by design. The round bevel has infinite slope at the rim: no jump, but c0ratio 2.26-2.78; smooth 7.93-7.98, linear 8.00. Chevron tiles are parallelograms, so hu is a bound. Period must be even for Basket and Chevron and a multiple of 2N for Herringbone, and Running needs off*P to be an integer.

Suggested, not tested here: TileSplit's Levels, Stop and Balance as an optional KD split on the box patterns.
tile-domain.port_notes: Each pattern is a small function returning (id, u, v, e, hu, hv), with no window. Herringbone: r=(i-j) mod 2N, r<N is horizontal starting at i-r, else vertical starting at j-(2N-1-r); this replaces the catalogue's 9 candidate search, tested for N=2, 3, 5. Hex: two rectangular lattices, take the nearer in hex norm. Scales: rows j0 and j0+1 are the only candidates. Fan: integer M sectors around the full circle hides the atan seam; compute the edge as rho*sin(hs-|th-thc|) with the same th that picked the sector; scale the atan polynomial by 1.00025877 so the octants meet. Frames must be rigid: one sin/cos for Fan, and add cs*slope*vv to u for Chevron.

master.one_liner: Closed-form structured tilings (running bond, herringbone, basket, hex, chevron, random-course ashlar, fan cobbles) that hand the Source per-tile local coordinates, a per-tile seed and an exact edge distance, so bricks, parquet, roof tiles, stone walls and honeycombs with per-tile variation become one node plus whatever Source you like.
master.look: Crisp regular masonry with controllable irregularity: stretcher-bond brick with per-brick colour and sunken bricks, herringbone/basket parquet with grain rotated per plank, hex honeycomb with bevelled walls, random-course stone walls where every stone has its own length and height but courses stay level, fan-pattern cobbles. In 3D the pattern is extruded along z with the tile seed, so per-column strata on z gives basalt columns and brick walls with thickness. Nothing on the contact sheet is structured and periodic with per-tile randomness.
master.algorithm:
Params: Pattern enum, TileW/TileH, N (brick length in units of width, Herringbone/Basket), RowOffset (hybrid; RunningBond), LengthJitter/HeightJitter (RandomCourses), Mortar (hybrid, world units), Bevel, Rotation enum {None, Quarter, Random(+-A)}, LookupScale, Output enum {Lookup, EdgeDistance, TileValue, TiltedHeight, LocalU, LocalV}, Source (GeneratorSource), MortarValue (hybrid).

Every pattern yields: integer tile id (i,j,extra), local (u,v) in [-0.5,0.5]^2 (normalised by the tile's own extents), edge distance e in world units. Then common post-processing.

Grid: i=floor(x/W), j=floor(y/H), u=x/W-i-0.5, v=y/H-j-0.5, e=min((0.5-|u|)W,(0.5-|v|)H).
RunningBond: j=floor(y/H); xs = x - RowOffset(j)*W with RowOffset(j)=off*j (0.5 = stretcher bond) or rnd01(j) (random bond); i=floor(xs/W); rest as Grid.
Basket: square s=(floor(x/(N W)), floor(y/(N W))); horizontal planks if (sx+sy)&1; plank index = floor(frac across * N); local coords with N:1 aspect; e from plank edges.
Hex: axial coords q=(2/3)x/R, r=(-1/3)x/R+(sqrt3/3)y/R, cube-round (3 rounds + 1 fix via masks) -> centre; e = R - max(|dy|, |dx| sqrt3/2 + |dy|/2) style hex SDF; (u,v) = offset/R.
Chevron: band b=floor(x/(N W)); sign = (b&1)? -1:+1; d=(sign*x+y)/sqrt2; strip k=floor(d/W); u along strip, v across; e = min(across distance, distance to band boundary).
Herringbone (1xN bricks): fundamental L = H brick [0,N)x[0,1) union V brick [N,N+1)x[0,N); lattice basis A=(-1,1), B=(N+1,N-1) (det = 2N = area, verified). (a,b) = M^-1 p; a0=floor(a), b0=floor(b); for (da,db) in {-1,0,1}^2: o=(a0+da)A+(b0+db)B, q=p-o; inH = 0<=q.x<N & 0<=q.y<1; inV = N<=q.x<N+1 & 0<=q.y<N; exactly one candidate hits; Select id, (u,v) (for H: (q.x/N-0.5, q.y-0.5); for V: (q.y/N-0.5, q.x-N-0.5)), e = min distance to the 4 brick edges. Proto should prune the 9 candidates to the 4 that can actually hit.
RandomCourses (ashlar / stacked stone / log pile / bookshelf): rows are a 1D jittered lattice on y: boundaries B_j=(j+HeightJitter*(rnd01(j)-0.5))*H, j found with the 4-boundary select (compute B_{k-1..k+2}, k=floor(y/H), row = k+1-[y<B_{k+1}]-[y<B_k]); within row j stones are a 1D jittered lattice on x seeded by j with per-row phase: C_i=(i+rnd01(j)+LengthJitter*(rnd01(i,j)-0.5))*W; stone = same select on x; (u,v) normalised by the actual stone width/height; e = min distance to its 4 boundaries. 8 hashes total; vertical joints never align across courses.
Fan (European fan cobbles): staggered fan cells (RunningBond with off 0.5, pitch P); in each fan, polar coords about the fan's bottom-centre: rho=|q|, theta via polynomial atan2 (seam at +-pi lies on the clipped fan base); ring k=floor(rho/ring), cobbles per ring m_k=round(pi(k+0.5)ring/cobble), cobble index floor(theta/pi*m_k) -> cobble centre -> dome or edge distance; fans overlap, higher row wins where rho<=P (2 rows x 2 columns candidates).

Common post: H=hash(i,j,extra,seed); e' = e - Mortar; inside = e'>0; TileValue = rnd11(H); Rotation: Quarter rotates (u,v) by (H&3)*90deg via swaps/negations, Random rotates by A*rnd11(H) (one sin/cos per lane); Lookup = Source.Gen(seed ^ H, (u*W+offX(H))*LookupScale, (v*H+offY(H))*LookupScale [, z, w]) selected with MortarValue outside, times smoothstep(0,Bevel,e') if Bevel>0; EdgeDistance = ScaleOutput(e'); TiltedHeight = HeightJitter*rnd11(H) + u*tx(H) + v*ty(H) (sunk / tilted tiles).
Nesting works because Lookup passes tile-local coordinates: TileDomain(Hex, Source=TileDomain(Grid,...)) = mosaic within tiles; TileDomain(Herringbone, Quarter, Source=wood rings) = parquet.
master.why_new: Checkerboard is the only structured lattice node. A graph cannot find the tile containing a point for bond/herringbone/hex/ashlar, cannot give the Source tile-local coordinates with a per-tile seed, and cannot produce an exact tile edge distance for mortar and bevels. Random courses in particular (rows of random-length elements) are a top texture-artist request with no graph equivalent.
master.simd_plan: Branch-free: floors, a few hashes, mask selects; Herringbone is 9 (prunable to 4) candidate parallelogram tests with integer/compare ops; Hex is cube-rounding with masks; RandomCourses is 8 hashes and two 4-way selects. No window search except Fan (4 candidates). 2D/3D/4D: the pattern lives in (x,y) and extra axes pass through to the Source with a per-tile offset (rotate the plane upstream with DomainRotate); GenTileable2D is not needed because the pattern is periodic by construction with an integer Period. Cost: Grid/Bond/Hex about 0.5-1 ns + Source, Herringbone/RandomCourses about 1.5 ns + Source, Fan 4-6 ns (Worley-like).
master.continuity: EdgeDistance mode C0 (min of distances). Lookup/TileValue/TiltedHeight are discontinuous at tile edges by design (it is a tiling); Bevel>0 makes Lookup C0 by forcing it to MortarValue at the edge.
master.params: Pattern enum, TileW/TileH, N int, RowOffset (hybrid), LengthJitter/HeightJitter, Mortar (hybrid, lets a noise erode the grout), Bevel, Rotation enum + Angle, LookupScale, Output enum, Source, MortarValue (hybrid), optional integer Period for hash wrap (explicit tiling).
master.risks:
Herringbone candidate pruning and the exact hex SDF need a proto check. Fan needs an atan2 polynomial (allowed) and its seam must stay on the clipped base. Many enum branches mean a long but shallow .inl; keep each pattern a small inlined function returning (id, u, v, e). Mortar as a hybrid can create tiny islands where e'<0 everywhere (fine).
[TilePattern, stamp-scatter] Herringbone and basketweave index math is fiddly; prototype in the scalar lab first. Aspect ratios other than 2:1 for herringbone need generalising. Per-tile seed discontinuities are the point, but the continuity check will WARN.
master.cost_note: Cost: Grid/Bond/Hex about 0.5-1 ns + Source, Herringbone/RandomCourses about 1.5 ns + Source, Fan 4-6 ns (Worley-like).

height-blend.look: Side by side on the same two sources the difference is obvious. Fade linear gives a see-through double exposure: ghost pebbles fogged over sand, rock fading into soil. HeightBlend keeps full contrast on both sides and the boundary follows the features: pebbles stay whole and stand out of sand, sand fills the gaps first, rock ridges survive longest into the soil. Fading on Control plus detail noise (the usual hand fix) also gives a crisp edge, but it slices pebbles in half because the edge knows nothing about them. Two plain fbms still interlock but look like a generic noisy border. Pavers against very fine fbm gives a salt-and-pepper dither band, because the height detail is at sample scale.
height-blend.dims: Generic over dimension: 2D and 3D measured, 4D has nothing dimension specific in the formula (not run).
height-blend.range: Convex combination of A and B, so it stays inside their range: pair 1 measured -0.592..0.986 over 8 seeds, pair 3 -0.888..0.906.
height-blend.artifacts: Inherits discontinuities from its sources: pair 0 reads c0ratio 1.00 only because the pebble source has per-cell jumps; continuous pairs read 6.62 and 7.39. Depth to 0 becomes a hard switch. Graph caveat: Fade(A, B, Fade = Add(Subtract(HB, HA), Multiply(2, Control)), FadeMin = 1 - Depth, FadeMax = 1 + Depth) matches it, with max difference 0.118 and std about 0.016 on all 4 pairs, and looks the same by eye. So it is a keeper for cost and ease, not for an otherwise impossible look.
height-blend.node_shape: HeightBlend: A, B, Control (hybrid), Fade Min, Fade Max (hybrid), Height A, Height B (optional hybrid; default = A and B outputs), Height Scale, Depth (hybrid). Output enum {Value, Weight, CompositeHeight}, so one blend can feed the next one's height.
height-blend.port_notes: GenT over the pack. When Height A and B are unconnected, reuse the A and B values already computed, which is where the speed gain comes from: the re-evaluating graph measured 670.2 vs 391.6 ns on pair 0 (1.71x) and 827.1 vs 503.2 ns on pair 3 (1.64x). From reading Modifiers.inl, not measured: GeneratorCache has one thread_local slot per instantiation, so two caches alternating A and B evict each other.

critic.notes: The look claim holds: on pebbles/sand and the mossy wall HeightBlend keeps both materials crisp and the border follows the features, Fade is a double exposure. Re-ran pair 3 with a noise control at seed 3: node and the Fade+Add+Subtract graph are identical by eye, c0ratio 7.3 / 7.9. So the look is a graph recipe; the case for a node is cost. I measured that with real nodes in fnlab AVX2: plain Fade of two 4-octave fractals 10.0 / 23.0 / 38.2 ns (2D/3D/4D), the HeightBlend graph re-evaluating both sources 21.4 / 48.7 / 68.6 ns, and wrapping every source in GeneratorCache 21.9 / 51.1 / 72.2 ns, so the cache does not rescue it (confirms the prototyper's code reading). A native version costs about a plain Fade, a 2x saving. That is worth having, but it is Fade with a height-aware weight, so it belongs as optional Height A / Height B hybrids and a Depth on Fade rather than a new node; a Weight output could be a Fade enum too. Inherits source jumps; fine height detail dithers.

master.one_liner: Terrain-splat style blend where the higher material wins inside a depth band, so one layer interlocks with the other instead of fogging over it.
master.look: Pebbles poke through sand; grass overtakes rock at its tips first; scree invades snow along cracks. Look-tested (mode 8): sheet Fade produces a foggy grey ramp, while HeightBlend gives a crisp interlocking cell-shaped boundary with full contrast on either side.
master.algorithm: t = sat((Control - FadeMin) / (FadeMax - FadeMin)). a = HeightA(p) + (1 - t); b = HeightB(p) + t. T = max(a, b) - Depth. wa = max(a - T, 0); wb = max(b - T, 0). out = (A(p)*wa + B(p)*wb) / (wa + wb). The taller layer always has weight Depth, so the denominator is positive for Depth > 0. Heights default to the (remapped) A and B outputs.
master.why_new: Fade is transparency, which is the main reason procedural biome borders look like mush. HeightBlend is the standard engine and tool answer (Unreal HeightLerp, splat shaders), but as a graph it needs two to four source copies, several Add/Max nodes and a Divide. As a node, it is a hard thing made trivial and likely among the most-used nodes for biome work.
master.simd_plan: Generic GenT, two Max and one division. Costs the sum of inputs and adds under 1 ns in any dimension. Reuse A and B values when heights are not separately connected to avoid double evaluation. Can apply batch-skip when all lanes have wa = 0 or wb = 0 (FS::AnyMask, as Terrace does).
master.continuity: C0 for Depth > 0 (measured c0ratio 5.8). Depth to 0 becomes a hard switch. Output stays within the range spanned by A and B because it is a convex combination.
master.params: A, B (generators), Control (hybrid), Fade Min, Fade Max (hybrid), Height A, Height B (hybrid), Depth (hybrid), Height Scale.
master.risks: Heights must share a scale with the fade range or one layer always wins. Depth too small gives aliasing. Skipping evaluation must stay exact for feature-set parity. Heights with very smooth content reduce to a plain threshold.
master.cost_note: Costs the sum of inputs and adds under 1 ns in any dimension.

queue.reason: Splat-style height-interlocking blend under 1 ns, what every material graph wants from Fade (J1 top pick). Low look risk; the must-have of the blend category.

textile.look: The weave is immediately cloth. Plain, 2/2 twill with its diagonal rib, 5 and 8 harness satin with long floats and isolated tie points, each with twisted fibre lines along the yarn. The relief view shows threads rising and diving over each other. Thin threads with no fibre give a very convincing wire mesh. Per-thread tone gives denim or plaid. The knit needed work: the catalogue stitch settings with the soft height rule looked like wavy rows, and only a=1.35, h=0.95, thin yarn, legs raised (d=-0.25) read as interlocking V chains. It now reads as a chunky stockinette at close range and as knit fabric in the wide view; close up it is a little rope-like. Thin yarn gives a chain fence. 3D volumes are real interlocking tubes. Warped twill looks like woven kelp; the same warp on knit shreds the loops and looks poor.
textile.dims: 2D measured as a heightfield. 3D measured as real yarn: Eval3 is 1 - d/r around the true 3D thread path, and the volume renders (knit and plain) show separate tubes passing over and under, with plies repeating along z. 4D not run. master.one_liner: One closed-form cloth node: woven threads with a linear over-under rule, or real interlocking knit loops solved from the textile stitch curve, with per-thread variation from 1D hashes.
master.look: Look-tested (mat_inv m=6 and m=14). Weave gives convincing plain, twill and satin with twisted thread shading. Knit reads immediately as interlocking stockinette loops; thinner yarn becomes chainmail. Good for fabric, wicker, chainmail, wire mesh, and as a bump layer under fractals. Warps turn it into draped cloth.
master.algorithm: Structure=Weave: i=floor(x), j=floor(y), f=fract, phase ph=mod(i*Step+j, N). Warp is over when ph<K; weft is over otherwise. (N,K,Step) gives plain (2,1,1), twill (4,2,1), satin (5,1,2). Warp crown coordinate cw=(ph+fy)/K when over, (ph-K+fy)/(N-K) when under, and z_warp=+/-sin(pi*cw). Weft uses fx the same way with the opposite sign. Per-thread hashes hi=hash(i), hj=hash(j) set width w=W*(1+WJ*rnd(h)) and wobble u=fx-.5+Wob*noise1D(y,hi). Height of each thread = 0.5*z + 0.5*sqrt(1-(u/w)^2) + Fibre*sin(F*(u+Twist*y)); output Max(warp,weft). Structure=Knit: stitch curve x(t)=t+a*sin(2t), y(t)=h*cos(t), z(t)=d*cos(2t). X=pi*x folded to |X-2pi*round(X/2pi)|. For each row j in a fixed window: start t0=acos(clamp((y-j)/h)), try branches t0 and 2pi-t0, run 2 Newton closest-point steps t+=clamp(dot(P-C,C')/dot(C',C'),-.7,.7) using sin 2t=2sc and cos 2t=1-2s^2. Then d^2=|P-C|^2, tube q=1-d^2/w^2, height=z(t)+0.55*sqrt(q), Max over rows and branches. Row hash gives yarn width and tone.
master.why_new: Nothing on the contact sheet has periodic structure with real over-under occlusion, and a graph cannot express the phase rule or the per-thread hashes. The knit curve has overhang, so it cannot be a height function of x. The closest-point solve is what makes it work pointwise.
master.simd_plan: Weave: one cell, 2 hashes, integer modulus for ph, Select for over/under, 2 sin plus one or two sqrt: scalar proto 4.4x Perlin including two 1D wobble evals, about 2x Perlin expected in AVX2. Knit: rows x 2 branches x 3 sincos pairs is 17x Perlin scalar with a 6 row window. Shrink to 3-4 rows (h<=0.8) and replace Newton with a small per-node polyline table of the folded half stitch (4-5 segments, built when params are set), target 6-8x Perlin. 3D: Z selects a ply (floor(z*Plies) hash shifts the phase and lateral offset) with a shell profile. 4D: W is a second ply index, so it is a real function but the torus map bends the pattern.
master.continuity: Discontinuous by design at occlusion edges (measured c0ratio 1.04 for weave), since one thread really passes over another. Inside each thread C1. A Softness param using MaxSmooth gives C0 at some cost in crispness.

master.risks: Lattice-locked pattern looks distorted through GenTileable2D's 4D torus; an integer Repeat param on (i,j) would give true tiling. fiber-noise.look: Dense capsules on a field Angle give the best fur image in the family, thick tapered locks sweeping in whorls, and they hold up in the relief view as overlapping tufts. Spread 1 gives straw or pine needles on a dark ground, low spread gives rain or brushed strokes. Density from a noise gives tufts that fade in smoothly instead of popping. The streak path gives long straight fibres with free ends, visually the same class as a 5x5 capsule window at a third of the cost. K=1 with an upstream warp gives combed hair or wood-grain lines with real swirl singularities. Very fine K=8 gives thin scratches. Nothing on the contact sheet has line features with free ends.
fiber-noise.dims: 2D and 3D measured. 3D capsule (27 cells, K=1) gives scattered needles; 3D streak path (K=6, 8 cells per layer) gives long crossing rods like hay. 3D XZ slices show dots and short dashes, as expected for thin lines cut by a plane. 4D not prototyped.
fiber-noise.range: -1..1 by construction, values measured -1.000..0.999 (fur) and -1.000..0.988 (streak K6). Output is sparse: mean -0.46 for fur, -0.78 to -0.84 for streak, so most samples sit at the floor. This is the nature of the look, and a graph usually Remaps or Adds it over a base.
fiber-noise.artifacts: The streak FFT is a star with K arms from orientation quantisation. Stamp jitter of 0.26 rad at K=6 spreads the arms but does not remove them; by eye K=6 reads as natural straw, while K=1 and K=2 read as deliberate directions. Bend on the streak path barely shows because the lateral budget clamps it. Field Angle fibres are not true streamlines: at field frequency 0.5 they become hooks and wisps. Thin lines alias at low sample rate. Saturated Sum shows bright knots where many fibres cross.
fiber-noise.node_shape: FiberNoise: Path enum {Capsule, Layers}, Per Cell or Layers K, Length, Width, Tip Taper, Length Jitter, Value Floor, Blend enum {Max, Sum}, Density (hybrid). Capsule: Angle (hybrid, sampled at the lane), Spread (hybrid), Bend. Layers: Layer Length, Layer Spacing, Angle Jitter, Layer Jitter, Base Angle. 3D bias: Axis X/Y/Z and Bias.
fiber-noise.port_notes: Stamp: tt = clamp(t,-LL,LL), r = tt/LL, width w*(1-tip*r^2), amplitude x (1-r^2), q = 1-((t-tt)^2+n^2)/w^2, value = q^2*tap*amp. Tapering amplitude gives C0: bisection found no jump above 0.0004 with reach inside the window. Window test against a wider window: capsule L<=1 and streak K6 (with jit 0.26 and with bend) differ by 0.0000; streak K1 tight by 0.0002; 3D streak by 0.0000. L=1.3 in 3x3 differs by 0.1526 with a 0.0879 jump, so the test detects violations and Length must clamp at 1. Layers along reach is A*(1-ju/2)-jit*latMax, lateral reach is S*(1-jv/2); clamp angle jitter and bend per stamp from the remaining budget. Density uses a soft threshold so fibres fade rather than pop.

master.one_liner: Sparse convolution with capsule kernels: thin tapered segments in a window, giving scratches, straw, hair and rain, bending seamlessly along a hybrid angle.
master.look:
Prototype cl_fiber: Spread 1 is straw or pine needles on a dark ground; Spread .15 is rain, brushed metal, grass tufts; a field Angle turns them into curled hooks and flowing fur strokes. Very sparse, high-kurtosis, totally unlike any contact-sheet field. Use for grass or hair density masks, scratches, leaf litter, wood fibre.
[FlowFibers, texture-materials] Look-tested (m=5). A striking result: flowing hair and combed fibre whirls with thamp=3.14, wood-pore streaks with thamp=0.8. Unlike anything on the sheet. Drive Angle from noise for hair, from a constant for brushed metal, from Gradient-like fields for grain. Coverage mask from another source for tufts.
master.algorithm:
Per cell c in 3^d window, K segments: h=hash(c,k); site uniform in cell; a=Angle(x)+Spread*(rnd-.5)*pi; u=(cos a,sin a); d=x-site; t=dot(u,d); n=dot(perp u,d)-Bend*rnd11*t^2 (parabola keeps it local); LL=L*(.5+.5*rnd); tt=clamp(t,-LL,LL); dist2=(t-tt)^2+n^2; WW=W*(.5+rnd)*(1-.7*(tt/LL)^2); q=1-dist2/WW^2; v=q>0?q^2*(.4+.6*rnd):0.
Output Max (or saturated Sum)*2-1.
Angle is sampled at x, not at the site, so all fibres bend in the field with no seams.
3D/4D: u from unit-vector table biased by an axis; n replaced by the perpendicular component of d, dist2=|d|^2-t^2+(t-tt)^2.
Constraint: LL+WW must be <= window reach (1 for 3^d; 2 for 5^d in 2D only).
master.why_new: The survey shows Lewis's hair kernel as the demo of sparse convolution, but no FastNoise node has line-like features. CellularDistance with Max metric or anisotropic scale cannot make thin isolated segments with free ends.
master.simd_plan: Per capsule: hash, 2 dots, Min/Max, 2 Selects, ~.6 ns. K=1: 9/27/81 capsules = ~5/18/65 ns; K=2 in 2D ~11 ns (10x Perlin; scalar prototype 7.5x). 4D needs 2^4 window with short segments, ~10 ns. Generic GenT possible with direction table.
master.continuity: C0 when amplitude tapers with t. The proto did not taper amplitude and measured c0ratio 1.49 from full-height needle tips; the formula above fixes that. Kinks at strand centre lines by design, a smooth profile makes it C1 inside each strand.
master.params: Int: K per cell. Float: L, W. Hybrid: Angle, Spread, Bend, Density. Enum: Blend, Window.
master.risks:
Very high frequency content, thin lines alias at low resolution; output mean is near -1. Long fibres need 5^d. High field variation makes strokes hook unnaturally (seen). 3D slices show dots and short dashes unless an axis bias keeps fibres in plane.
[FlowFibers, texture-materials] Strands are only approximately streamlines: rapid angle change (field frequency near 1/L) makes them kinked or broken. Thin lines alias at low sample rates. Cost scales with Per Cell, and dense felt needs 4-6.
[StrokeField, lattice-kernels] Reach is L + jitter + Cap so long strokes force a wider window (cost). Bending is not real path integration, and strong orientation gradients produce claws rather than parallel hairs (a look, but not fully controllable).
master.cost_note: K=1: 9/27/81 capsules = ~5/18/65 ns; K=2 in 2D ~11 ns (10x Perlin; scalar prototype 7.5x).
master.variant_notes: The bend comes for free: orientation is read once at the sample, so strokes curve along level sets of the field at one source eval. Taper amplitude as well as width, or tips jump (measured c0ratio 1.49 without).

level-set-weave.look: Good look, but not a separate node. Warped axes give a hand-made basket with bulging threads. Two low frequency noises give flowing strands like muscle or kelp, with crossings stretched where the two fields' gradients run parallel. A polar pair gives a wicker base with no visible seam when spokes is an even integer. Two Worley F1 fields give woven concentric rings of constant width, which is the most striking one and unlike anything on the sheet. At high thread counts everything turns into a moire op-art pattern rather than cloth. The deciding test: the Textile weave run on the same A and B reproduces the plain case almost identically and adds twill and satin, with better threads.
level-set-weave.dims: 2D measured. 3D measured and unimpressive: the volume is the pattern extruded into ribbons along z, and the shell volume breaks into separate lumps. Textile's 3D tubes are the real 3D answer. 4D follows from the sources, not run.
level-set-weave.range: -1.000..1.000 over 8 seeds on warped axes, two Worley, and Textile on two Worley.
level-set-weave.artifacts: Thread width follows 1/|grad A|, as warned: two-noise plates have fat and pinched bands. A per-lane width correction from the analytic gradient kept widths constant but left black voids, which looked worse, so I dropped it. True distance inputs (Worley F1) give constant width without correction. Per-Worley-cell polar has real jumps at cell borders (c0ratio 1.08). Two Worley with the catalogue profile measures c0ratio 7.97. The round thread profile on two noises measures 3.12, about the sqrt(8) a rim gives, so I read it as a rim rather than a jump.
level-set-weave.node_shape: Not its own node. Textile gains two optional sources A and B (defaulting to x and y) and Threads k.
level-set-weave.port_notes: The Textile weave on (A*k, B*k) needs no changes (mode=2): c0ratio 7.97 with prof=1 on two Worley, range -1..1. The fibre term runs along the field coordinate, so fibre density follows the same gradient as thread width.

master.one_liner: Over-under textile weave driven by two arbitrary fields: threads are level-set bands of A and B, and parity decides which lies on top.
master.look: Tested with a hillshade. With warped axes it reads clearly as woven basket or cloth with visible over-under, puckered threads. With two noises it gives flowing, stacked strands like bark, muscle fibre or woven kelp. Unlike anything on the sheet. Uses: fabric, wicker, chainmail bases, stylised terrain folds, roots.
master.algorithm:
u=A(p)*k; v=B(p)*k; iu=Floor(u); iv=Floor(v); fu=u-iu; fv=v-iv.
par=1-2*((iu+iv)&1).
prof(t)=Cos(pi*Clamp((t-0.5)/gap,-0.5,0.5)).
ha=prof(fu)*(0.5+0.5*par*Cos(pi*(fv-0.5)));
hb=prof(fv)*(0.5-0.5*par*Cos(pi*(fu-0.5)));
Out=Max(ha,hb), remapped to [-1,1].
Optional thread colour: Select(ha>hb, hash(iu), hash(iv)) gives plaid. A=x+warp and B=y+warp gives warped cloth; two low-frequency noises give flowing bark-like weave.
master.why_new: Checkerboard plus warp gives colour cells, never a height relief with threads that cross over and under. Doing this as a graph would need floor, parity and select nodes, none of which exist. Any two node graphs can drive it, not just axes.
master.simd_plan: Branch free, integer parity bit test. 2 source evals + 4 Cos, replaceable by even polynomials. Estimated under 2x the source cost + 1 ns. 3D: A,B level sets become sheets, which give a ribbon structure; optional C source and a max of 3 terms for a triaxial weave. 4D is the same formula via sources.
master.continuity: C0, verified numerically (ratio 8.0), with creases along Max(ha,hb) where threads meet. Not C1, as with real thread crossings.
master.params: A, B sources (hybrid so constant offsets work). Hybrid: Threads k, Gap. Enum: Height, Plaid Id.
master.risks: Thread width scales inversely with |grad A| because the bands are not distance-normalised, so low-gradient regions show fat threads (visible in the two-noise plate). Piping sources through IsoBands distance would fix that at extra cost. The 3D look is unverified. Requires large noise amplitude on A,B to get many threads.
master.cost_note: Estimated under 2x the source cost + 1 ns.

master.one_liner: Long, randomly oriented ribbons that are several cells long without breaking the window rule: K orientation layers, each with its own anisotropic (stretched) lattice aligned to that layer's direction, each cell holding one elongated stamp that fits its long cell.
master.look:
Prototype at 6 layers: crossed hairline scratches, tapered, varying brightness, like brushed metal, sword wear, straw, pine needles, rain, cross-hatching. Long continuous structures of a kind no isotropic node makes, and the staple missing mask for material work.
[StreakScatter, stamp-scatter] Brush strokes, scratches on metal, wood splinters, grass blades, hatching, rain streaks on glass, needle beds, fibre mats, frost feathers; K=1 gives a combed/hair look, K=4 gives criss-cross scratches, K=8 looks isotropic. Elongated features with random orientation and visible ends are absent from the contact sheet (DomainAxisScale gives stretched noise but every feature is parallel and endless).
master.algorithm:
Layers k = 0..K-1 (K is an int param, fixed loop), direction angle a_k = pi*k/K + LayerJitter(seed,k) (constant per layer, computed when params are set or from a hash of k). For each layer: rotate p into the layer frame (u along a_k, v across), scale u by 1/Length so the lattice cell is Length x 1 in world units. Run the Scatter 2^2 window in (u,v). Each stamp is a capsule/ribbon: local coords q = (u', v'/Width) with per-stamp small angle jitter (+/- pi/(2K)) applied before the lattice lookup, per-stamp length fraction in [0.5,1], per-stamp seed. Stamp profile: gaussian across the ribbon, smooth taper along it (optionally a Source node evaluated in the ribbon frame, e.g. a 1D-ish Perlin along u for bristle wobble), optional along-ribbon sine for scratches. Combine stamps within a layer and across layers by Max/Sum/SmoothMax.
3D: directions on the sphere via a fixed set of K unit vectors (Fibonacci sphere, table), lattice stretched along each; stamps are capsules in 3D (hairs, roots, needles). 4D: use the 3D directions and treat w as a 4th unstretched lattice axis (tiling works).
Why it is seamless: in the layer frame every stamp is confined to a 1 x 1 lattice cell exactly as in Scatter; the stretch happens in the domain, not in the stamp.

[ScratchLayers, stamp-scatter] For layer l in Layers (constant): table rotation a_l chosen at param set. u = (cos a x - sin a y)/Spacing + o_u, v = (sin a x + cos a y)/(Spacing*A) + o_v. Cell (iu,iv), window 3x3. Each cell: alive if rnd<Prob; centre cu = iu + 0.25 + 0.5*rnd, cv = iv + rnd; slope s in +-0.3 and bend b in +-0.15 cells over the unit v, chosen so lateral excursion stays below 1 cell (essential for seamlessness). Curve line: u0(v) = cu + s*(v-cv) + b*(v-cv)^2; half length hl in [0.25,0.95] of a long cell; tv = (v-cv)/hl. Width w = Thick*(power-law random)*sat(1-tv^2). dist = |u-u0|. Profile = sat(1-dist/(w+soft))*sat(1-tv^2). Combine by max across all. 3D: lattice 1x1xA (27 cells per layer), distance sqrt(du^2+dw^2) gives rods, fibers, needles.
master.why_new: A long oriented feature cannot fit a square lattice window, so plain Scatter cannot do it, and DomainAxisScale on a noise makes all features parallel. Quantising orientation into K layers and stretching each layer's lattice is the trick that keeps it pointwise. Gabor noise does something related with a Poisson process but produces sine blobs, not shaped strokes with ends.
master.simd_plan: K x (2D: 4 cells) with ~50 ops per cell; K=4 in 2D ~5 ns, K=8 ~10 ns. 3D K x 8 cells, K=6 ~30 ns. Layer frames are precomputed when params are set (rotation matrices in a small table). Branch free; K is a fixed loop count. Per-stamp angle jitter is a small rotation inside the cell, kept within the cell by reducing the stamp length fraction accordingly.
master.continuity: C0 verified: c0ratio 7.87 after limiting lateral excursion; first version with excursion above the window gave real seams (c0ratio 1.04), confirming the constraint.
master.params: Layers int K, Length (cells), Width, Angle Jitter, Length Jitter, Taper, Profile enum (Gaussian/Flat/Sine scratch/Source), Source (optional), Combine enum, Density hybrid (sampled at stamp centre), Feature Scale, Seed Offset.
master.risks:
K orientation classes are visible at small K (hatching look) — fine for most uses, add LayerJitter so angles are not exactly uniform. Cost scales with K; cap at 8. 3D direction set of K vectors must be chosen well to avoid obvious preferred axes.
[ScratchLayers, stamp-scatter] Thin features alias at coarse sampling, like any line. Width smaller than a pixel means Feature Scale and output sample rate need thought. Fixed-angle layers give a limited orientation set when Layers is small, which is visible; Slope helps. Value of 4D modest.
master.cost_note: K x (2D: 4 cells) with ~50 ops per cell; K=4 in 2D ~5 ns, K=8 ~10 ns. 3D K x 8 cells, K=6 ~30 ns.
master.variant_notes: Rotated anisotropic lattices per layer. A 1:A lattice keeps long strokes inside a 3x3 window; lateral excursion must stay below 1 cell or real seams appear (measured c0ratio 1.04 before that fix).
